I'm mapping out the grid nodes at rows and columns 1,4,7,10,13, then tracing each orange marker's direction to determine where it points—down, left, or right—to find its destination node on the grid.

Following these directions, I trace a path starting at (4,1) through (4,4), (7,4), (10,4), (10,7), (7,7), (4,7), (4,10), (1,10), continuing onward, and I notice the path eventually loops back on itself, forming a cycle starting at (10,7).

Now I'm mapping out this cycle's edges into grid segments so I can draw them, working through column and row spans one by one.

Building grid rows...

Continuing down, rows 8 and 9 mirror the earlier pattern with column 7 and 13 marked, while row 10 has a wider stretch across columns 7-13 all set to 1, and row 11 comes out all zeros.

I'm sketching out a second test grid, reusing the same row/column lattice structure but designing a new cycle of arrow directions connecting nodes in sequence, starting from a different node and color.

Now I'm assigning arrow orientations to every remaining node so each one points to a valid in-bounds neighbor, checking that none point off the grid and that the start node (7,2) correctly feeds into the cycle rather than being part of it.

Continuing to verify remaining nodes each have exactly one adjacent orange cell, confirming the grid works at 10 rows by 14 columns. Now I'm thinking about designing a second demo with a different cycle shape and color, sketching a larger cycle across rows 1,4,7 and columns 2,5,8.

Working through the arrow paths, I realize corner-to-corner arrows would pass through intermediate nodes, so I need the cycle to explicitly include edge midpoints — building it as (1,2)→(1,5)→(1,8)→(4,8)→(7,8)→(7,5)→(7,2)→(4,2)→back to (1,2), ensuring every segment only passes through one node at a time.

Checking the remaining adjacencies confirms each orange marker touches exactly one neighbor, so the second cycle is verified on this 9×11 grid. That gives two solid cycles, which should be enough, but I'll consider a third smaller rectangular cycle with a different color on interior nodes to round things out.

I'm double-checking adjacency for each orange-colored node against its neighbors to confirm no conflicts, then moving on to build the 9x11 grids.
